title: A File Format to Aid in Security Vulnerability Disclosure
subtitle: A plain text file at a known address that tells researchers how to report a security hole.
summary: security.txt is a small, machine-readable text file that an organization publishes at /.well-known/security.txt on its website. It lists where to send vulnerability reports, which encryption key to use, where the disclosure policy lives, and when the information goes stale. The goal is to make it easy for a researcher who has found a problem to find the right person to tell.

plainLanguage.summary: security.txt is a small machine-readable text file that an organization publishes at /.well-known/security.txt on its website. It lists where to send vulnerability reports, which encryption key to use, where the disclosure policy is, and when the information expires. It helps a researcher who has found a flaw to reach the right contact.

tldr.problem: Researchers who find a vulnerability often cannot tell who owns the affected site or how that owner wants to be told.
tldr.mechanism: The owner serves a UTF-8 text file at /.well-known/security.txt with Contact and Expires fields plus optional pointers to a policy, an encryption key and a hall of fame.
tldr.outcome: Reports reach the right people, and the Expires field and optional OpenPGP signature let readers discard stale or tampered files.

today: security.txt files are widely published by large technology companies, public-sector bodies and many smaller sites, and generators and validators for the format are easy to find. Because the RFC is an Informational document from the IETF stream rather than a standards-track specification, adoption rests on convention and tooling rather than on any protocol requirement.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 9116 defines "security.txt", a text file that an organization places in a known location to describe its vulnerability disclosure practices. In the RFC's words, many researchers "are unable to report security vulnerabilities to organizations because there are no reporting channels" and no information about how the owner handles disclosure.

The format is machine parsable and must follow the ABNF grammar in Section 4 of the RFC. It is deliberately narrow: it covers how to reach the organization and what to expect, and leaves the rest of vulnerability handling to other documents such as ISO/IEC 29147 and the CERT Guide to Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure.

The file is meant for "vulnerability response", meaning reports about product flaws. It is not intended for incident response about intrusions or compromised websites, and the RFC warns about extra risks if you use it that way.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 9116 defines security.txt, a text file that describes an organization's vulnerability disclosure practices. Many researchers cannot report flaws because no reporting channel is published. The format is machine parsable and deliberately narrow, covering only how to reach the organization. It is meant for reports about product flaws, not for incident response about intrusions.

sections.title: Motivation and prior work
sections.content:
Before this RFC there were several contact conventions, but none answered the researcher's question for an arbitrary organization. RFC 2142 sets the convention of a SECURITY@domain mailbox, but that is a single email-based channel and says nothing about the owner's disclosure practices. RFC 3013 covers contacts for Internet service providers, RFC 2350 covers incident response teams, and RFC 2196 covers site operators. Registries publish contact data for IP address, ASN and domain owners under RFC 7485.

The RFC states that "none of these tackle the issue of how security researchers can locate contact information and vulnerability disclosure practices for organizations in order to report vulnerabilities." security.txt is described as complementary to other public resources and not a replacement for them.

The table below compares the approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: Earlier conventions did not answer a researcher's question for an arbitrary organization. RFC 2142 suggests a SECURITY@domain mailbox but says nothing about disclosure practices. Other RFCs cover contacts for service providers, response teams and site operators, and registries hold contact data for IP address and domain owners. security.txt complements these and does not replace them.

sections.title: File format
sections.content:
The file is plain text, encoded as UTF-8 in Net-Unicode form. It is a list of fields, one per line, each written as a name, a colon, a space and a value, such as Contact: mailto:security@example.com. Field names are case-insensitive. A field must have a name and a value, must appear on its own line, and may appear more than once unless its definition says otherwise.

A line that starts with # is a comment. Blank lines are allowed. Every line ends with either CRLF or just LF. The values of most fields are URIs, so email addresses must be written as mailto: URIs and phone numbers as tel: URIs.

Readers must ignore any field they do not support, which keeps the format extensible through an IANA registry. The example below is the unsigned file from the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The file is plain UTF-8 text made of fields, one per line, written as a name, a colon, a space and a value, such as Contact: mailto:security@example.com. Field names are case-insensitive. Lines starting with # are comments. Most values are URIs, so email addresses use mailto: and phone numbers use tel:. Readers must ignore fields they do not support.

sections.title: The fields
sections.content:
Unless stated otherwise every field is optional. Two are mandatory: Contact must always be present, and Expires must always be present and must not appear more than once. Contact values should be listed in order of preference, the first being the preferred method.

Encryption must be a URI that points to a key, and keys must not appear in the field itself. Canonical lists the URIs where the file is meant to live. Policy links the disclosure policy, Acknowledgments links a page crediting researchers, and Hiring links the organization's security-related jobs. Preferred-Languages is a comma-separated list of language tags, appears at most once, and defaults to English if absent.

Wherever a field holds a web URI it must begin with https://. The Expires value uses the RFC 3339 date-time profile, and the RFC recommends keeping it less than a year in the future.
sections.plainLanguage: Two fields are mandatory: Contact, listed in order of preference, and Expires, which appears once. Other fields point to an encryption key (Encryption), the disclosure policy (Policy), a credit page (Acknowledgments), security jobs (Hiring) and the file's own locations (Canonical). Preferred-Languages defaults to English. Web URIs must start with https://, and Expires should be less than a year ahead.

sections.title: Location and scope
sections.content:
For web services the file must live under the /.well-known/ path, for example https://example.com/.well-known/security.txt, as defined by RFC 8615. For legacy compatibility a copy may also sit at the top-level path /security.txt, or that path may redirect to the well-known one. If both exist, the well-known copy must be used.

The file must be fetched with HTTP 1.0 or higher over the https scheme and must be served with a Content-Type of text/plain with charset utf-8.

A file applies only to the domain or IP address in the URI used to retrieve it, "not to any of its subdomains or parent domains". It may also apply to products and services the organization provides. The RFC's examples include a file at a subdomain that covers only that subdomain, and files served from IPv4 and IPv6 literal addresses. The Policy field is the place to spell out finer scope.
sections.plainLanguage: For web services, the file must be at /.well-known/security.txt, fetched over https and served as text/plain in UTF-8. A copy or redirect at /security.txt is allowed for legacy compatibility. The file applies only to the domain or IP address it was fetched from, not to its subdomains or parent domains. The Policy field can set finer scope.

sections.title: Trust and security considerations
sections.content:
A file that tells people where to send secrets is a tempting target. An attacker who has compromised a website can change the file or add a redirect, so reports are lost or sent to the attacker. The RFC advises organizations to list Canonical URIs, to sign the file, and to monitor it. It recommends signing with an OpenPGP cleartext signature (RFC 4880, Section 7). If the retrieval URI is not in any Canonical field, the file should not be trusted.

Staleness is also a risk, so "not having a security.txt file may be preferable to having stale information in this file." Researchers are told to record redirects, to validate certificates, and to guard parsers: the RFC suggests they may refuse files larger than 32 KB, fields longer than 2,048 characters, or more than 1,000 lines.

Researchers should not assume that the presence or absence of a security.txt file grants or denies permission for security testing. Any such permission may instead be stated in the disclosure policy or a new field.

Other noted risks include multi-tenant hosts where another user could take over the path, and the extra spam that publishing a contact address invites.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker who compromises a site can alter the file or redirect it, so reports go astray. The RFC advises listing Canonical URIs, signing the file with an OpenPGP cleartext signature and monitoring it. A file served from a URI not in any Canonical field should not be trusted. Stale information is worse than no file. Having or lacking the file does not grant or deny permission to test.

sections.title: IANA registrations
sections.content:
The RFC makes two registry changes. First, it adds security.txt to the Well-Known URIs registry with change controller IETF and status permanent. Second, it creates a new "security.txt Fields" registry managed with Expert Review under RFC 8126.

The initial registry holds the eight fields defined in the RFC, all with status "current". Acknowledgments, Canonical, Contact, Encryption, Hiring and Policy may appear multiple times; Expires and Preferred-Languages may not. Any field registered later is optional, and readers must ignore fields they do not understand. This is how the format can grow without breaking old parsers.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds security.txt to the Well-Known URIs registry and creates a new "security.txt Fields" registry. It starts with the eight fields the RFC defines. Fields registered later are optional, and readers must ignore fields they do not understand, so the format can grow without breaking old parsers.

data.title: https://example.com/.well-known/security.txt
data.code:
# Our security address
Contact: mailto:security@example.com

# Our OpenPGP key
Encryption: https://example.com/pgp-key.txt

# Our security policy
Policy: https://example.com/security-policy.html

# Our security acknowledgments page
Acknowledgments: https://example.com/hall-of-fame.html

Expires: 2021-12-31T18:37:07z

items.title: Sign the file
items.text: An OpenPGP cleartext signature lets researchers authenticate the content.

items.title: List Canonical URIs
items.text: A signed Canonical field ties the file to the location it was served from.

items.title: Set a near Expires
items.text: Less than a year ahead, so stale contacts are not used.

items.title: Harden parsers
items.text: Cap size, field length and line count, and record redirects.
